steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our robotics paper on fusing GPS with visual-inertial odometry while calibrating the rotation between the GPS and VIO frames online. Cover why neither GPS nor VIO/SLAM is enough alone, the observability question for this rotation, and our contributions.

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
1. GPS for robot localization and its limits
- accurate, robust, reliable pose estimation essential for safe autonomous navigation of mobile robots
- GPS widely used outdoors for decades: robust global localization, no accumulated drift
- consumer grade GPS: high-level noise -> GPS alone not accurate
- urban scenes: interference, signal occlusions, bounces off high-rise buildings
- GPS-degraded/-denied: VIO (IMU + camera(s)) and SLAM used instead

2. VIO and SLAM drawbacks; case for fusion
- VIO: no interruptions, high-precision, high-frequency local estimation
- but no long-term drift-free localization and heading
- VIO has four unobservable DoF: 3D positions and yaw
- SLAM: joint localization + map, loop-closure, map alignment -> less uncertainty and drift
- SLAM: high computational and memory demands
- GPS + visual inertial navigation -> accurate, high frequency, robust, long-term drift-free; GPS + camera + IMU fusion promising

3. Observability of the GPS-VIO transformation
- GPS-aided VIO already proposed
- GPS-VIO frame transformation unobservable under linear observability analysis
- linearization -> local result, may be unreliable for the nonlinear system
- revisit with nonlinear observability analysis; aim: rotational extrinsic is observable

4. Proposed system and contributions
- filter-based GPS-VIO system; reliable, accurate estimation of rotation extrinsic between GPS and VIO frames
- estimator fusing GPS + visual-inertial data, online rotational extrinsic estimation
- observability proof via nonlinear analysis, backed by simulations
- evaluation on public datasets: small scale flying, large scale driving; superior performance

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Accurate, robust and reliable pose estimation is essential for mobile robots to navigate autonomously and safely. For the past few decades, the Global Positioning System (GPS) has been widely used for localization in outdoor scenes, because it gives a robust global localization solution that does not accumulate drift over time. However, consumer grade GPS sensors have high-level noise, so accurate positioning typically cannot be achieved with GPS sensors alone. Also, in urban scenes, GPS signals are vulnerable to interference from the local environment, like signal occlusions or bounces because of high-rise buildings, and this degrades the GPS positioning performance even more. In these GPS-degraded or -denied scenarios, what is conventionally implemented is Visual-Inertial Odometry (VIO) using an IMU (Inertial Measurement Unit) and Camera(s), and Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (SLAM) algorithms.

VIO algorithms are not affected by these interruptions, and they give high-precision and high-frequency local state estimation, but they have inherent drawbacks too. For instance, VIO systems cannot give long-term drift-free localization and heading. Prior work proves that VIO systems have four unobservable Degrees of Freedom (DoF), which are the 3D positions and yaw. SLAM reduces this drawback by estimating the localization and the map at the same time, along with loop-closure and map alignment. With these mechanisms SLAM techniques can decrease the localization uncertainty and the long-term drift. Unfortunately, SLAM techniques need a lot of computational and memory resources, and this limits where they can be applied. In general, GPS positioning and a visual inertial navigation system can be combined to give accurate, high frequency, robust and long-term drift-free localization. Fusing the three sensors involved, GPS, camera and IMU, has given promising results and can achieve localization that is locally accurate and globally drift-free.

Observability of the GPS-VIO transformation
- GPS-aided VIO already proposed
- GPS-VIO frame transformation unobservable under linear observability analysis
- linearization -> local result, may be unreliable for the nonlinear system
- revisit with nonlinear observability analysis; aim: rotational extrinsic is observable

Proposed system and contributions
- filter-based GPS-VIO system; reliable, accurate estimation of rotation extrinsic between GPS and VIO frames
- estimator fusing GPS + visual-inertial data, online rotational extrinsic estimation
- observability proof via nonlinear analysis, backed by simulations
- evaluation on public datasets: small scale flying, large scale driving; superior performance

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Accurate, robust and reliable pose estimation is essential for mobile robots to navigate autonomously and safely. For the past few decades, the Global Positioning System (GPS) has been widely used for localization in outdoor scenes, because it gives a robust global localization solution that does not accumulate drift over time. However, consumer grade GPS sensors have high-level noise, so accurate positioning typically cannot be achieved with GPS sensors alone. Also, in urban scenes, GPS signals are vulnerable to interference from the local environment, like signal occlusions or bounces because of high-rise buildings, and this degrades the GPS positioning performance even more. In these GPS-degraded or -denied scenarios, what is conventionally implemented is Visual-Inertial Odometry (VIO) using an IMU (Inertial Measurement Unit) and Camera(s), and Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (SLAM) algorithms.

VIO algorithms are not affected by these interruptions, and they give high-precision and high-frequency local state estimation, but they have inherent drawbacks too. For instance, VIO systems cannot give long-term drift-free localization and heading. Prior work proves that VIO systems have four unobservable Degrees of Freedom (DoF), which are the 3D positions and yaw. SLAM reduces this drawback by estimating the localization and the map at the same time, along with loop-closure and map alignment. With these mechanisms SLAM techniques can decrease the localization uncertainty and the long-term drift. Unfortunately, SLAM techniques need a lot of computational and memory resources, and this limits where they can be applied. In general, GPS positioning and a visual inertial navigation system can be combined to give accurate, high frequency, robust and long-term drift-free localization. Fusing the three sensors involved, GPS, camera and IMU, has given promising results and can achieve localization that is locally accurate and globally drift-free.

GPS-aided VIO algorithms have been proposed before in the literature. With linear observability analysis, the spatial transformation that couples the GPS and the VIO reference frame is shown to be unobservable. But linearization means that the derived observability is only local, and it may not be reliable for the original nonlinear system. So the observable property needs to be revisited with nonlinear observability analysis. More specifically, in this paper we want to show that the rotational extrinsic parameter between the GPS reference frame and the VIO reference frame is observable.

In this paper, we propose a new filter-based GPS-VIO system that focuses especially on estimating the rotation extrinsic between the GPS reference frame and the VIO reference frame reliably and accurately. Our key contributions are:

- We propose a new filter-based estimator that fuses GPS measurements and visual-inertial data and at the same time estimates the rotational extrinsic parameter between the GPS and VIO frames online.

- We prove with nonlinear observability analysis that the rotational extrinsic parameter is observable, and we support this conclusion with simulations.

- We evaluate the localization accuracy of the proposed algorithm on multiple public datasets, including small scale flying datasets and large scale driving datasets, and show that our algorithm performs better.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Accurate, robust and reliable pose estimation is essential for the safe autonomous navigation of mobile robots. In the past few decades, the Global Positioning System (GPS) has been widely used for localization in outdoor scenes, since it gives a robust global localization solution without accumulating drift over time. However, due to the high-level noise of consumer grade GPS sensors, accurate positioning cannot be typically achieved by using GPS sensors alone. Also, in urban scenes, GPS signals are vulnerable to the interference of the local environment, such as signal occlusions, or bounces due to high-rise buildings, which further degrades the GPS positioning performance. In these GPS-degraded or -denied scenarios, Visual-Inertial Odometry (VIO) using IMU(Intertial Measurement Unit) and Camera(s), and Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (SLAM) algorithms are conventionally implemented.

VIO algorithms are not affected by these interruptions, and provide high-precision and high-frequency local state estimation, however, these algorithms also have their inherent drawbacks. For instance, VIO systems cannot provide long-term drift-free localization and heading. In [1], the authors prove that VIO systems have four unobservable Degrees of Freedom (DoF), namely the 3D positions and yaw. SLAM reduces this drawback using simultaneous estimation of the localization, the map, along the execution of the loop-closure, and map alignment. These mechanisms allow SLAM techniques to decrease the localization uncertainty and the long-term drift. Unfortunately, SLAM techniques need high computational and memory resources, which limits where they can be applied. In general, GPS positioning and visual inertial navigation system can be combined to provide an accurate, high frequency, robust localization and long-term drift-free localization. Fusing the three sensors involved in this process, GPS, camera and IMU has given promising results and can achieve locally accurate and globally drift-free localization.

GPS-aided VIO algorithms have been proposed before in the literature [2,3]. The spatial transformation to couple both the GPS and the VIO reference frame is shown to be unobservable with linear observability analysis [2,4]. However, linearization implies that the derived observability is local and may be unreliable for the original nonlinear system [5,6]. So it is necessary to revisit the observable property with the tool of nonlinear observability analysis. More specifically, we aim to show in this paper that the rotational extrinsic parameter between GPS reference frame and VIO reference frame is observable.

In this paper, we propose a novel filter-based GPS-VIO system which focuses especially on a reliable and accurate estimation of the rotation extrinsic between the GPS reference frame and the VIO reference frame. Our key contributions are:

- • We propose a novel filter-based estimator to fuse GPS measurements and visual-inertial data, and simultaneously estimate the rotational extrinsic parameter between the GPS and VIO frames online.

- • We prove that the rotational extrinsic parameter is observable via nonlinear observability analysis, and support our conclusion with simulations.

- • We evaluate the localization accuracy of the proposed algorithm on multiple public datasets, including small scale flying datasets and large scale driving datasets, and show that our algorithm performs better.

References:
[1] J. Kelly and G. S. Sukhatme, “Visual-inertial sensor fusion: Localization, mapping and sensor-to-sensor self-calibration,” The International Journal of Robotics Research , vol. 30, no. 1, pp. 56–79, 2011.
[2] W. Lee, K. Eckenhoff, P. Geneva, and G. Huang, “Intermittent gps-aided vio: Online initialization and calibration,” in 2020 IEEE International Conference on Robotics and Automation (ICRA) , pp. 5724–5731, IEEE, 2020.
[3] G. Cioffi and D. Scaramuzza, “Tightly-coupled fusion of global positional measurements in optimization-based visual-inertial odometry,” in 2020 IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS) , pp. 5089–5095, IEEE, 2020.
[4] W. Lee, K. Eckenhoff, P. Geneva, and G. Huang, “Gps-aided visualinertial navigation in large-scale environments,” Robot Perception and Navigation Group (RPNG), University of Delaware, Tech. Rep , 2019.
[5] W. J. Terrell, “Local observability of nonlinear differential-algebraic equations (daes) from the linearization along a trajectory,” IEEE Transactions on Automatic Control , vol. 46, no. 12, pp. 1947–1950, 2001.
[6] Y. Tang, Y. Wu, M. Wu, W. Wu, X. Hu, and L. Shen, “Ins/gps integration: Global observability analysis,” IEEE Transactions on Vehicular Technology , vol. 58, no. 3, pp. 1129–1142, 2008.
